title: AraHalluEval: A Fine-grained Hallucination Evaluation Framework for Arabic LLMs
license: CC BY 4.0 (paper text, ACL Anthology); datasets/code licensed separately
key_findings: First broad hallucination evaluation of 12 Arabic, multilingual and reasoning LLMs on Arabic generative QA and summarisation, using 12 fine-grained hallucination indicators.
Factual hallucinations were more frequent than faithfulness errors (unfaithfulness to the given source) across all models and tasks.
The Arabic pre-trained model ALLaM showed consistently lower hallucination rates than multilingual models and was comparable to reasoning models.
athar_applications: Supports ATHAR's choice to feed characters only a closed fact pack (faithfulness setting) rather than relying on model world-knowledge.
Gives an indicator taxonomy to adapt for ATHAR's dialogue validator test set; ALLaM is a candidate to include in Arabic pilot tests.
limitations: Tasks are QA and summarisation in MSA, not role-play or dialect dialogue; no minors; model versions will age quickly.

title: HalluTruthQA: A Fine-Grained Benchmark for Hallucination Detection, Localization, and Explanation in Arabic Question Answering
license: CC BY 4.0 (paper text, ACL Anthology); datasets/code licensed separately
key_findings: 2,400 expert-curated Arabic QA examples (Islamic knowledge, history, science, geography) with hallucination labels, character-level error spans and explanations.
No single open model (ALLaM-7B, Falcon-H1R-7B, Qwen3-32B, SILMA) was best on all tasks; best macro-F1 for binary detection 0.880 but span-localisation F1 only 0.516.
athar_applications: Binary 'is this answer hallucinated' checks are far more reliable than locating the exact wrong phrase: ATHAR's validator should flag whole turns and fall back to authored lines rather than try to edit spans.
limitations: Knowledge QA, not closed-world fiction; zero-shot setting only; 2026 conference paper not yet replicated.

title: Arabic Safety Alignment as Selective Refusal: An Empirical Study of SFT, DPO, and Guard Calibration
license: CC BY 4.0 (paper text, ACL Anthology); datasets/code licensed separately
key_findings: Separates harmful-prompt refusal (H) from benign over-refusal (B): refusal-only fine-tuning collapsed toward refusing everything, while selected mixed configurations reached H about 90-93% with B 14-23%.

Guards and DPO shifted H and B differently per model rather than acting as uniform upgrades; Qwen3Guard and Aya Expanse 32B reached about 89-91% accuracy against a human refusal audit (kappa 0.78 between annotators).
Safety gains in MSA transferred only partly to Arabizi: no model reached 90% harmful refusal on Arabizi.
athar_applications: ATHAR must report two numbers for its teen safety layer: missed-harm rate and over-refusal of legitimate mystery content (crime themes are central to the product).
Arabizi and dialect inputs need their own test slice; MSA results cannot be assumed to transfer.
limitations: Adult/general prompts (AraSafe), not minors; 2026 paper; operating points are model-specific.

title: ArGuard Shared Task: Harmful Content Detection in Arabic Memes and LLM Prompts
publisher: Association for Computational Linguistics (ArabicNLP 2026 Shared Tasks)
license: CC BY 4.0 (paper text, ACL Anthology); datasets/code licensed separately
key_findings: Shared task with a track (B) on detecting harmful Arabic prompts aimed at LLMs; 35 teams in final evaluation.

Best macro-F1 was 0.984 for binary safe/unsafe prompts but 0.790 for fine-grained harm categories; participant papers report large drops from development to blind test (one team fell from 0.946 to 0.639) and poor zero-shot results on Darija for a generative Arabic model.
athar_applications: Binary input screening in Arabic is feasible with fine-tuned encoders; fine-grained routing (e.g., self-harm vs violence) is much less reliable, so ATHAR's crisis routing must not depend on a single fine-grained classifier.
Released datasets can seed ATHAR's Arabic red-team set (licence to be checked).
limitations: Prompts are general-adult harm, not teen-specific; distribution shift between dev and test is large; per-dialect results only in some team papers.

title: Some Dialects are More Equal than Others: Non-Prestigious Arabic Dialectal Bias in LLMs
license: CC BY 4.0 (paper text, ACL Anthology); datasets/code licensed separately
key_findings: LLMs showed a significant preference against Sa'idi (Upper Egyptian) dialect features compared with prestigious Cairene Egyptian Arabic.
Accuracy on MMLU-style questions often degraded when the same content carried Sa'idi features.
athar_applications: Dialect fairness tests for ATHAR (scorer, safety filter, character understanding) must include sub-dialects and rural/non-prestige varieties, not one variety per country.
limitations: One sub-dialect pair; adult knowledge questions; no scoring of learner writing.

title: Saudi-Alignment Benchmark: Assessing LLMs Alignment with Cultural Norms and Domain Knowledge in the Saudi Context
license: CC BY 4.0 (paper text, ACL Anthology); datasets/code licensed separately
key_findings: 874 curated questions on Saudi cultural/ethical norms and domain knowledge; GPT-4 83.3%, ALLaM-7B 81.8%, Llama-3.3-70B 81.6%, Jais-30B 21.9%.
Models did better on selected-response formats than on generative answers, so recognition-style benchmarks may overstate cultural alignment.
athar_applications: Cultural appropriateness of character dialogue must be tested generatively (open dialogue), not only with multiple-choice probes.
limitations: Single country; adult knowledge; no safety-for-minors dimension.

title: Halluscoring 2026: The First Shared Task on LLM Hallucination Detection Answer Verification
publisher: Association for Computational Linguistics (ArabicNLP 2026 Shared Tasks)
license: CC BY 4.0 (paper text, ACL Anthology); datasets/code licensed separately
key_findings: Arabic hallucination detection degraded under distribution shift: winning AUC-ROC was 0.772 for unseen questions and 0.767 for answers from unseen LLMs.
Selecting the correct answer from six candidates reached 0.882 (Islamic knowledge) and 0.857 (general knowledge) under assisted evaluation.
athar_applications: A learned Arabic hallucination detector cannot be ATHAR's primary guard: with AUC near 0.77 on new models, ATHAR keeps the deterministic closed-world validator (fact IDs, entities, numbers) as the primary control.
limitations: Open-world factual QA, not fiction; 13 teams; results tied to 2026 models.

title: Same Legal Facts, Different Verdicts: Evaluating Cross-Lingual and Dialectal Robustness in LLM Legal Reasoning
license: CC BY 4.0 (paper text, ACL Anthology); datasets/code licensed separately
key_findings: 200 bar-exam-style questions held constant across English, formal Arabic, simplified Arabic and Egyptian Arabic.
All models scored highest in English; GPT-4o was most stable (90% English, 80-82% Arabic variants) while one frontier model fell from 80.5% to 17.5-21% in Arabic.
athar_applications: Model selection for ATHAR must be based on Arabic and dialect versions of ATHAR's own tasks; English leaderboard rank is not predictive.
Each localized case version is a new test item (consistent with DAR-MGSM finding).
limitations: Legal multiple-choice, adult domain; small item set; specific model snapshots.

title: Jailbreaking LLMs with Arabic Transliteration and Arabizi
license: CC BY 4.0 (paper text, ACL Anthology); datasets/code licensed separately
key_findings: AdvBench prompts in standard Arabic, even with prefix injection, did not readily produce unsafe output from GPT-4 and Claude 3 Sonnet.
The same prompts written in Arabic transliteration or Arabizi (chat alphabet) did elicit unsafe content on both platforms.
athar_applications: Teens commonly type Arabizi; ATHAR's input safety layer must normalise or separately classify Arabizi and transliterated text, and the red-team set must include Arabizi attacks.
limitations: Model versions from 2024; attack success not reported per teen-relevant category; describes vulnerability, not mitigation efficacy.

title: AraTrust: An Evaluation of Trustworthiness for LLMs in Arabic
license: CC BY 4.0 (paper text, ACL Anthology); datasets/code licensed separately
key_findings: 522 human-written Arabic multiple-choice questions covering truthfulness, ethics, privacy, illegal activity, mental and physical health, unfairness and offensive language.
GPT-4 scored highest; open models AceGPT-7B and Jais-13B stayed below 60%. Dataset released on Hugging Face under MIT licence.
athar_applications: Provides an MIT-licensed Arabic item set for a pre-screen of candidate models before ATHAR's own dialogue red-teaming; includes mental-health items relevant to crisis handling.
limitations: Multiple-choice knowledge of safe behaviour is not the same as safe generation in role-play; small; adult framing.

title: Low-Resource Languages Jailbreak GPT-4
publisher: NeurIPS 2023 Workshop on Socially Responsible Language Modelling Research (SoLaR)
key_findings: Translating unsafe English AdvBench prompts into low-resource languages bypassed GPT-4 safeguards 79% of the time.
Modern Standard Arabic was classed as high-resource; its bypass rate was about 3.65%, far below low-resource languages (combined high-resource rate about 11%).
athar_applications: Standard MSA is not the weakest point; the real Arabic risk surface is non-standard input (Arabizi, transliteration, dialect, code-switching) and mixed-language prompts, which ATHAR's red-team set must emphasise.
limitations: Workshop paper; GPT-4 2023 snapshot; MSA only; translation via API.

title: All Languages Matter: On the Multilingual Safety of LLMs
publisher: Association for Computational Linguistics (Findings of ACL 2024)
license: CC BY 4.0 (paper text, ACL Anthology); datasets/code licensed separately
key_findings: XSafety covers 14 safety issue types in 10 languages including Arabic; all four tested LLMs gave more unsafe answers to non-English queries than English ones.
Arabic was among the less safe languages: unsafe rates of 9.2% (ChatGPT), 17.4% (PaLM-2) and 56.6% (Vicuna) versus 1.0%, 10.3% and 6.0% in English for the same models (arXiv v2 table).
A prompting method improving cross-lingual safety generalisation cut ChatGPT's non-English unsafe ratio by 42%.
athar_applications: Baseline expectation for ATHAR: Arabic unsafe-response rates can be several times English rates for the same model; safety must be measured in Arabic, not inferred from vendor English evaluations.
limitations: 2023-era models; translated prompts; adult-oriented categories.

title: The Multilingual Alignment Prism: Aligning Global and Local Preferences to Reduce Harm
license: CC BY 4.0 (paper text, ACL Anthology); datasets/code licensed separately
key_findings: Introduced human-annotated multilingual red-teaming prompts distinguishing 'global' from 'local' (culturally specific) harms; the released Aya red-teaming dataset includes Arabic and is Apache-2.0 licensed.
Showed alignment methods can reduce harm across 6 languages with minimal loss of general performance.
athar_applications: ATHAR's teen-safety taxonomy should have a 'local harm' layer written with Arab child-protection experts (e.g., honour, sectarian, family-shaming content) in addition to global categories.
limitations: Not child-specific; Arabic is one of several languages; alignment results are for Cohere-trained models.

title: Arabic Dataset for LLM Safeguard Evaluation
license: CC BY 4.0 (paper text, ACL Anthology); datasets/code licensed separately
key_findings: 5,799 Arab-region-specific questions: direct attacks, indirect attacks and harmless requests containing sensitive words.
Dual-perspective evaluation (governmental vs opposition stance) on sensitive topics; five Arabic-centric and multilingual LLMs showed substantial disparities in safety performance.
athar_applications: Harmless-with-sensitive-words items are the right template for testing over-refusal of legitimate crime-mystery talk in ATHAR.
Political/religious stance questions should be routed to authored deflections in ATHAR rather than generated.
limitations: Adult; politically sensitive framing may not transfer to every market; not a role-play setting.

title: MinorBench: A Hand-Built Benchmark for Content-Based Risks for Children
key_findings: Case study of an LLM chatbot deployed in a middle school documented how students used and misused it.
Proposes a taxonomy of content risks specific to minors and an open benchmark; six LLMs showed substantial variability in child-safety compliance depending on the system prompt.
athar_applications: Use the minors' risk taxonomy as a starting point for ATHAR's teen safety categories, translated and localised; system-prompt wording measurably changes child-safety behaviour, so it is a versioned, tested artefact.
limitations: English only; Singapore context; workshop paper.

title: Safe-Child-LLM: A Developmental Benchmark for Evaluating LLM Safety in Child-LLM Interactions
key_findings: 200 adversarial prompts for two developmental bands (7-12 and 13-17) with human-annotated jailbreak success and a 0-5 ethical refusal scale.
Reports critical safety deficiencies across major commercial and open models in child-facing scenarios.
athar_applications: Graded (0-5) refusal quality scale is a usable template for scoring ATHAR's authored safety exits, beyond binary refused/not-refused.
limitations: Preprint, not peer-reviewed; small; English; prompts drawn from adult red-team corpora.

title: SproutBench: A Benchmark for Safe and Ethical Large Language Models for Youth
key_findings: 1,283 developmentally grounded adversarial prompts across three age bands (0-6, 7-12, 13-18) probing emotional dependency, privacy violations and imitation of hazardous behaviour; 47 LLMs evaluated.
Reports an inverse relationship between interactivity and age-appropriateness of responses.
athar_applications: Adds emotional-dependency and imitation-of-hazard probes to ATHAR's red-team set (relevant to suspect/companion characters and forensic content).
limitations: Preprint; English; automated judging details not verified here.

title: Multilingual Jailbreak Challenges in Large Language Models
key_findings: Distinguishes unintentional (user simply writes in a non-English language) from intentional multilingual jailbreaks.
Unsafe output rose as language resource level fell; low-resource languages were about three times as likely to yield harmful content as high-resource ones for ChatGPT and GPT-4.
MultiJail dataset: 315 unsafe prompts translated by native speakers into 9 languages, Arabic classed as medium-resource; released under MIT licence.
athar_applications: The 'unintentional' scenario is exactly a teen typing in dialect; ATHAR's test set should include benign-intent dialect messages touching sensitive topics, not only adversarial ones.
MIT-licensed Arabic subset can be used in internal red-team regression tests.
limitations: 2023 models; translation of English prompts rather than native Arabic harms.

title: AraSafe: Benchmarking Safety in Arabic LLMs
publisher: Association for Computational Linguistics (Findings of EMNLP 2025)
license: CC BY 4.0 (paper text, ACL Anthology); datasets/code licensed separately
key_findings: First large native Arabic safety benchmark: 12K naturally occurring human-written prompts, double-annotated into nine categories (e.g., illegal activities, violence or harm, privacy violation, hate speech), plus 12K synthetic harmful prompts.
Benchmarked Arabic-centric and multilingual 7-13B models (Jais, AceGPT, ALLaM, Fanar, Llama-3, Gemma-2, Qwen3) and BERT classifiers, finding critical safety blind spots.
athar_applications: Preferred base corpus for ATHAR's Arabic input-safety evaluation because prompts are native, not translated; nine-category scheme maps onto ATHAR's teen taxonomy.
limitations: General-population prompts, not minors; 84% MSA, 16% dialect, no Arabizi; contributors two-thirds Egyptian, 62% female, all university-educated. Dataset released for academic non-commercial use (paper's ethics statement) - not for training a commercial product without permission. [Corrected 2026-10-27 by deep-card review: earlier text said 'licence to confirm'.]

title: Child Helpline International - Middle East and North Africa member helpline profiles (Saudi Arabia, UAE, Egypt, Jordan, Lebanon, Kuwait, Qatar, Morocco)
key_findings: Network directory profiles list, per member: operator, services/channels, languages and opening hours; fetched 2026-10-27.

Listed MENA members relevant to ATHAR markets: Saudi 116111 (NFSP, 07:00-23:00), UAE DFWAC 800111 (24/7) and Sharjah 800700, Egypt 16000 (NCCM, 24/7), Jordan JRF 110 (not 24/7), Kuwait 147, Qatar Aman 919 (24/7), Morocco EMC helpline; Lebanon members (Higher Council for Childhood, Naba'a) list no phone line. Bahrain and Oman have no CHI profile in the listing.
athar_applications: Primary cross-check for 11_RIGHTS_PRIVACY_AND_SAFETY/YOUTH_HELPLINE_REGISTER.csv; each number must also be confirmed on an operator or government page and test-called by a local partner before shipping in the crisis exit.
limitations: Directory may lag operator changes (e.g., Kuwait 147 had a documented outage in 2019); hours/languages self-reported by members.

title: Llama Guard 3 (8B) model card - supported languages
key_findings: Model card states content-safety support for eight languages: English, French, German, Hindi, Italian, Portuguese, Spanish and Thai - Arabic is not listed.
Llama Guard 4 card states its multilingual text support follows the same Llama Guard 3 language set.
athar_applications: The Llama-Guard pattern cited in AI_CHARACTER_GUARDRAILS R13 [ATH-SRC-0955] cannot be deployed as-is for Arabic; ATHAR needs an Arabic-capable guard (e.g., one listing Arabic) and its own dialect/Arabizi evaluation.
limitations: Vendor documentation; language list may change in later releases; absence from list does not mean zero Arabic performance, only no stated support.

title: PolyGuard: A Multilingual Safety Moderation Tool for 17 Languages
publisher: arXiv (preprint) / Hugging Face model card ToxicityPrompts/PolyGuard-Qwen
license: CC BY 4.0 (model card/weights as declared on Hugging Face)
key_findings: Open multilingual safety classifier trained on 1.91M samples in 17 languages; Arabic (ar) is among the declared languages.

Releases PolyGuardPrompts, a 29K-sample multilingual benchmark mixing natural multilingual interactions with human-verified translations of WildGuardMix; authors report outperforming open and commercial classifiers by 5.5%.
athar_applications: Candidate open-weight Arabic-capable guard for ATHAR's safety_in/safety_out layer, to be benchmarked against AraSafe/ArGuard and an ATHAR teen slice before adoption.
limitations: Preprint; translated data dominate; no dialect- or teen-specific results verified here.

title: Qwen3Guard-Gen-8B model card
license: Apache-2.0 (model weights, per model card)
key_findings: Generative guard model claiming support for 119 languages and dialects, with three severity tiers: safe, controversial, unsafe.
An independent Arabic study found Qwen3Guard about 88.7% accurate against a human refusal audit [ATH-SRC-1602].
athar_applications: The 'controversial' tier maps naturally onto ATHAR's need to allow crime-mystery themes while routing sensitive content to authored lines rather than hard refusal.
limitations: Vendor claims; Arabic dialect and teen-specific performance not documented on the card.

title: ARNLI: Arabic Natural Language Inference Entailment and Contradiction Detection
publisher: AGH University of Science and Technology Press (Computer Science journal)
license: CC BY 4.0
key_findings: Built ArNLI, an Arabic contradiction-detection dataset of over 12K sentences.
Best classical model reached 75% accuracy on ArNLI (and 60% on a machine-translated SICK set), illustrating how hard Arabic contradiction detection remains.
athar_applications: Confirms that ATHAR's R8 NLI contradiction check cannot assume the ~74% English balanced accuracy of SummaC [ATH-SRC-0942] transfers; Arabic NLI must be benchmarked on ATHAR's own testimony pairs.
Dataset is a candidate seed for an Arabic contradiction-test set (licence to check).
limitations: Pre-LLM methods; MSA; sentence pairs not dialogue; no dialect data.

title: XNLI: Evaluating Cross-lingual Sentence Representations
license: CC BY 4.0 (paper text, ACL Anthology); datasets/code licensed separately
key_findings: Extended MultiNLI dev/test sets to 14 additional languages including Arabic, creating a standard cross-lingual NLI benchmark.
Translating test data into English gave the best baseline at the time, showing cross-lingual inference was weaker than English.
athar_applications: Ready-made Arabic NLI evaluation set for checking any NLI model before using it in ATHAR's contradiction validator (R8).
limitations: Professional translations of English premises (MSA, not dialect); 2018 baselines outdated; genre differs from dialogue testimony.

title: METAL: Towards Multilingual Meta-Evaluation
publisher: Association for Computational Linguistics (Findings of NAACL 2024)
license: CC BY 4.0 (paper text, ACL Anthology); datasets/code licensed separately
key_findings: Native-speaker judgments of summaries in 10 languages including Arabic used to meta-evaluate GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and PaLM2 as judges; GPT-3.5 was poor, GPT-4 best.

For Arabic, GPT-4 agreement with human aggregates was around 0.69-0.71 F1 on linguistic acceptability and content quality versus 0.85-0.89 among humans (arXiv table); evaluator reasoning often did not match human reasoning.
athar_applications: An LLM judge for Arabic feedback/dialogue quality must be meta-evaluated per language and per metric before use; ATHAR's judge for character style (R-style oracle) needs an Arabic human-agreement study.
limitations: Summarisation only; 100 Arabic items; 2023 models.

title: Are Large Language Model-based Evaluators the Solution to Scaling Up Multilingual Evaluation?
publisher: Association for Computational Linguistics (Findings of EACL 2024)
license: CC BY 4.0 (paper text, ACL Anthology); datasets/code licensed separately
key_findings: Calibrated LLM evaluators against 20K human judgments across three generation tasks, five metrics and eight languages.
LLM evaluators were biased toward higher scores; calibration with native-speaker judgments is needed especially for low-resource and non-Latin-script languages.
athar_applications: Expect LLM graders of Arabic free text to be lenient; ATHAR's scorer acceptance test must check mean score inflation versus human raters, not only correlation.
limitations: Arabic inclusion among the eight languages not confirmed from the abstract page; summarisation/generation tasks, not student answers.

title: TAQEEM 2025: Overview of The First Shared Task for Arabic Quality Evaluation of Essays in Multi-dimensions
publisher: Association for Computational Linguistics (ArabicNLP 2025 Shared Tasks)
license: CC BY 4.0 (paper text, ACL Anthology); datasets/code licensed separately
key_findings: First Arabic essay-scoring shared task: holistic (Task A) and seven-trait (Task B) scoring on a new dataset of 1,265 Arabic essays.
Only five teams submitted runs across both tasks, reflecting how small the Arabic AES research community remains.
athar_applications: Provides a public benchmark and trait schema; ATHAR's reasoning traits (evidence use, alternatives, calibration) are absent and must be added in ATHAR's own annotation.
limitations: Essays are argumentative writing by (mostly) university-level Qatari writers; no dialect variable; linguistic traits.

title: Fine-tuning Small Language Models for Cross-Prompt Arabic Essay Scoring: A Benchmarking Study
license: CC BY 4.0 (paper text, ACL Anthology); datasets/code licensed separately
key_findings: First Arabic cross-prompt AES benchmark with Arabic-centric LLMs (ALLaM 7B, Jais 8B, Fanar 9B) in zero-shot, few-shot and fine-tuned settings.
Fine-tuning substantially improved all models; fine-tuned Fanar was state of the art on LAILA (+8 points over the strongest baseline) and generalised to ZAEBUC.
athar_applications: Supports ATHAR's plan to fine-tune a small Arabic model per task type for scoring rather than prompting a frontier model; cross-prompt generalisation is what ATHAR needs because each case is a new prompt.
limitations: Essay writing traits, not reasoning; adult/university writers; MSA.

title: Feature Engineering is not Dead: A Step Towards State of the Art for Arabic Automated Essay Scoring
license: CC BY 4.0 (paper text, ACL Anthology); datasets/code licensed separately
key_findings: Released the first public engineered feature set for Arabic AES (surface, readability, lexical, syntactic, semantic) and tested it on 620 essays with holistic and trait scores.
The feature set was competitive with recent neural methods including LLMs.
athar_applications: Interpretable features let ATHAR monitor whether scores track surface fluency (length, vocabulary) rather than reasoning - a direct check on the 'eloquent but empty' risk.
limitations: Small dataset; essay quality not reasoning; MSA.

title: Evaluating Prompt Relevance in Arabic Automatic Essay Scoring: Insights from Synthetic and Real-World Data
license: CC BY 4.0 (paper text, ACL Anthology); datasets/code licensed separately
key_findings: First Arabic benchmark for binary prompt-essay relevance (on/off-topic).
A fine-tuned SBERT reached 98% F1 on synthetic pairs and outperformed SVMs and threshold baselines on QAES+ZAEBUC, as a resource-efficient alternative to LLMs.
athar_applications: A cheap off-topic gate before scoring: ATHAR can reject answers unrelated to the case question before any LLM call, reducing gaming and cost.
limitations: Off-topic pairs created by mismatching prompts; essays not short answers; MSA.

title: In-Context Meta-Learning vs. Semantic Score-Based Similarity: A Comparative Study in Arabic Short Answer Grading
license: CC BY 4.0 (paper text, ACL Anthology); datasets/code licensed separately
key_findings: Compared instance-based (in-context meta-learning) and reference-based (semantic similarity to model answers) Arabic short-answer grading.
Both beat baselines; the reference-based method was stronger zero-shot and occasionally exceeded human raters on unseen answers.
athar_applications: ATHAR's short justifications can be scored against authored reference answers per case (reference-based), which needs little per-case training data.
limitations: Small dataset; GPT-3.5-era augmentation; no dialect or age analysis.

title: ZAEBUC: An Annotated Arabic-English Bilingual Writer Corpus
license: CC BY 4.0 (paper text, ACL Anthology); datasets/code licensed separately
key_findings: Short essays by first-year Zayed University (UAE) students in Arabic and English with spelling/grammar correction, morphology, POS, lemma and CEFR ratings.
Publicly available; later used as a cross-dataset test for Arabic AES.
athar_applications: Closest public corpus to young Gulf writers; useful for testing ATHAR's scorer robustness to real student spelling and grammar errors.
limitations: University first-years, not 13-18; essays not reasoning tasks; dialect features not annotated as such.

title: ZaQQ: A New Arabic Dataset for Automatic Essay Scoring via a Novel Human-AI Collaborative Framework
license: CC BY 4.0
key_findings: Used LLMs with trait-specific prompts, calibrated on QAES, to annotate ZAEBUC and QALB essays on seven traits, producing the merged ZaQQ dataset.
Authors claim human-AI collaboration expands labelled data without loss of assessment quality.
athar_applications: Cautionary pattern: LLM-labelled training data can propagate LLM grader biases; ATHAR's reference set must be human double-scored, with LLM labels used only for augmentation after audit.
limitations: Validation of LLM-generated labels against independent humans not verified here; MDPI data journal.

title: Rethinking LLM Evaluation with 3C3H: AraGen Benchmark and Leaderboard
key_findings: Arabic generative leaderboard scored by an LLM judge on six dimensions (correctness, completeness, conciseness, helpfulness, honesty, harmlessness).
Judge selection reported Cohen's kappa with a human judge of only 0.46 for the best judge (GPT-4o-mini), with Claude-3.5-Sonnet close; run-to-run score standard deviation was small for most judges.
athar_applications: Even the best Arabic LLM judge reached only moderate agreement with a human (kappa about 0.46); ATHAR must not display LLM-judged scores on Arabic free text to learners without its own human-agreement study.
limitations: Blog post, not peer-reviewed; single human annotator comparison details limited; adult Q&A.

title: Degree of Possessing Critical Thinking Skills by Students of Faculty Science and Arts Ola Depending on Test California 2000
title_ar: درجة امتلاك طلبة كلية العلوم والآداب بالعلا لمهارات التفكير الناقد تبعاً لاختبار كاليفورنيا (2000)
publisher: An-Najah National University (An-Najah University Journal for Research - B, Humanities)
key_findings: Administered the CCTST (form 2000) to 380 Saudi university students after checking its psychometric properties and suitability for the Saudi context.
Inference ranked highest among sub-skills; female students outscored males; no difference by specialisation.
athar_applications: Confirms an Arabic-administered CCTST exists in Saudi research use, but only with university students; no adolescent norms, so it cannot serve as ATHAR's external criterion for 13-18.
limitations: Psychometric details only summarised in abstract; licensing of the Arabic form not described; university sample.

title: The validity indices of item answer-key of the Egyptian version of Watson and Glaser critical thinking test and its effect on the psychometric properties of the test items and test reliability
title_ar: دلالات صدق مفتاح الإجابة عن مفردات الصورة المصرية لاختبار واطسون وجليسر في التفكير الناقد وأثره في الخصائص السيكومترية لمفردات الاختبار وثباته
publisher: Kuwait University (Educational Journal / al-Majalla al-Tarbawiyya), vol. 35, no. 140, pt. 2
key_findings: Examined the 1973 Egyptian adaptation (Jabir and Hindam) of the Watson-Glaser test with 459 Minia University students.
14 items had a doubtful answer key on all indicators; changing keys altered item-total correlations in 73 items, item difficulty/discrimination and test reliability.
Author recommends updating the test and its scenarios to fit contemporary Egyptian culture.
athar_applications: Strong warning against using legacy Arabic translations of commercial CT tests as ATHAR's criterion: answer keys and cultural content can be invalid in today's context.
limitations: University students; specific to the 1973 Egyptian form.

title: Differential item function and its impact on the differential test function using item response theory models and multiple group confirmatory factor analysis (Watson-Glaser short form)
title_ar: الأداء التفاضلي للبنود وتأثيره على الأداء التفاضلي للإختبار باستخدام نماذج نظرية الإستجابة للمفردة والتحليل العاملي التوكيدي متعدد المجموعات
publisher: Journal of Educational Sciences and Human Studies (Yemen), vol. 6, no. 15, pt. 1
key_findings: Applied 2PL IRT and nonparametric (Ramsay) DIF methods to the Arabic Watson-Glaser short form with 396 Qassim University (Saudi) students.
Many items showed DIF favouring science majors and some favouring humanities majors; multi-group CFA showed item DIF accumulated into test-level differential functioning.
athar_applications: Direct evidence that academic track biases an Arabic CT instrument; ATHAR's DIF checks must include school track (science vs humanities), not only gender, country and dialect.
limitations: University sample; single institution; journal quality unverified.

title: Using the Rasch Model to arranging a test of critical thinking: Watson-Glaser test for critical thinking short form
title_ar: إستخدام نموذج راش في تدريج اختبار التفكير النقدي: اختبار واطسون- جليسر للتفكير الناقد الصورة القصيرة
publisher: Journal of Psychological and Educational Sciences (Algeria), vol. 7, no. 3
key_findings: Rasch (1PL) scaling of a 34-item Arabic Watson-Glaser short form with 231 Algerian university students (Saida and Chlef).
Data fitted the Rasch model, no item was removed, and the authors report acceptable validity and reliability.
athar_applications: Shows Rasch calibration of Arabic CT items is feasible with a few hundred respondents - a realistic template for calibrating ATHAR's own pre/post probe items in Phase 2.
limitations: Small university sample; item content is commercial (not reusable); fit-only evidence.

title: Validation of Sherouk's Critical Thinking Test (SH-CTT)
publisher: IGI Global (Research Anthology on Developing Critical Thinking Skills in Students)
key_findings: Arabic-origin story-based CT test (four stories with agree/disagree items) validated on 158 university students; total reliability 0.885 and acceptable CFA fit per part.
athar_applications: Story-plus-scene item format resembles ATHAR's case format, but the sample and evidence are too thin to serve as a criterion.
limitations: Small adult sample; author-developed; reprint in an IGI anthology; no adolescent data.

title: Measuring cognitive reflection without maths: Development and validation of the verbal cognitive reflection test
license: CC BY 4.0 (article); item list hosted on OSF
key_findings: Developed a 10-item verbal CRT with low familiarity; good criterion/construct validity, internal consistency and test-retest reliability.
Less associated with numeracy and maths anxiety than the original CRT, measurement-equivalent across gender and age groups; no gender gap (g = -0.06) versus g = 0.29 on the original CRT.
athar_applications: Best-documented open option if ATHAR needs a cognitive-reflection covariate: a translated and re-validated verbal CRT avoids the maths confound that would disadvantage weaker-numeracy teens. No Arabic validation found.
limitations: Adult samples; Arabic translation would need full re-validation; items may become familiar.

title: Exhibit A.1: Country Participation in TIMSS 2023 and in Earlier TIMSS Assessments
publisher: TIMSS & PIRLS International Study Center, Boston College / IEA
key_findings: TIMSS 2023 grade 8 participants include Bahrain, Jordan, Kuwait, Morocco, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, UAE (with Abu Dhabi, Dubai and Sharjah benchmarking) and the Palestinian National Authority; Iraq took part at grade 4 with non-comparable data.
Egypt and Lebanon are not listed as TIMSS 2023 participants.
athar_applications: Most ATHAR markets have national grade-8 achievement and context data that can serve as covariates or sampling frames for Phase 2; Egypt and Lebanon lack this comparator.
limitations: Mathematics and science achievement, not reasoning or CT; participation table only.

title: TIMSS & PIRLS Copyright Notice (released items and publications)
key_findings: All IEA publications and released items, and translations of them, are for non-commercial, educational and research purposes only; prior notice to IEA is required when using IEA data sources for assessments or learning materials.
Commercial exploitation, reproduction or redistribution of released items requires written IEA permission; IEA cannot authorise third-party copyrighted content inside items.
athar_applications: ATHAR must not embed TIMSS/PIRLS released items (or Arabic translations) in the commercial product; research-only use in a university-led validation study requires notice to IEA, and commercial use requires a written licence.
limitations: Notice text current as of 2025 page; PISA (OECD) terms are separate and were not readable (oecd.org blocked automated access).

title: PISA 2025 Results (Volume I) - country notes and Arab participants (Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Jordan, Morocco, UAE)
key_findings: OECD published PISA 2025 Results Volume I on 8 September 2026 with country notes for, among others, Saudi Arabia and Qatar; 91 countries/economies took part.

Jordan's official agency (Petra) reported significant gains since 2022 (science 375 to 407, mathematics 361 to 388, reading 342 to 363); press reports place the UAE first among Arab participants and Morocco's scores down since 2022, with 'computational problem solving' assessed for the first time.
athar_applications: PISA 2025 adds a new domain (learning in the digital world/computational problem solving) close to ATHAR's process-assessment model [ATH-SRC-0650]; national results can frame school-partner conversations but are not a criterion for individual reasoning skill.
limitations: Country-note pages returned only metadata to automated tools; score figures for Jordan/Morocco come from government/press reports, not read on OECD pages; OECD licence for released items not verified.

AUDIT-W2 2026-10-27: OECD pages return HTTP 403 to curl; WebFetch confirmed the Saudi country note 'PISA 2025 Results (Volume I): Saudi Arabia' dated 8 Sep 2026. 91 countries/economies confirmed via the Swedish OECD delegation news page; Jordan scores 375->407, 361->388, 342->363 confirmed on petra.gov.jo. The 'computational problem solving' and UAE/Morocco claims were not re-verified (press-only). Verification remains search/secondary-based.

title: The impact of science teaching strategies in the Arabic-speaking countries: A multilevel analysis of TIMSS 2019 data
key_findings: Multilevel analysis of TIMSS 2019 grade-4 science in seven Arabic-speaking countries: about half of achievement variance lies between classrooms.
Emphasis on academic success and active instruction related positively to achievement, while investigation methods (planning and running experiments) related negatively, though effects were small.
athar_applications: Inquiry activities in typical Arab classrooms are not associated with higher achievement - consistent with the need for guided inquiry and explicit debriefs in ATHAR, and a caution against claiming that 'investigation' alone teaches.
Large between-class variance means ATHAR's classroom trials need cluster designs (supports Phase 6 ICC assumptions).
limitations: Correlational; grade 4 (not 13-18); teacher-reported strategies; achievement not reasoning.

title: The science of teaching science: An exploration of science teaching practices in PISA 2015
publisher: OECD Publishing (OECD Education Working Papers No. 188)
key_findings: Across PISA 2015 systems, enquiry-based science teaching was negatively associated with science performance, but the association was greatly attenuated in disciplined classes.
Teacher-directed instruction was positively associated with outcomes regardless of climate; all strategies could foster enjoyment, self-efficacy and interest.
athar_applications: Inquiry in ATHAR should be structured (clear goals, scaffolds, debrief) and classroom mode should give teachers control - unstructured exploration is the condition linked to weaker outcomes.
limitations: Cross-sectional, student-reported practices; science achievement not reasoning; not specific to Arab samples.

title: Understanding Verbal Probability Expressions: How Secondary School Students Interpret Probability Language
publisher: Springer (International Journal of Science and Mathematics Education)
license: CC BY 4.0
key_findings: 184 English secondary students rated 29 verbal probability expressions on a 0-100% slider; expressions near certainty or moderate probability showed most variability, those near 50% or low probability more agreement.
Older students gave more consistent and polarised interpretations, closer to adult data; no gender differences; proposes a benchmarking framework for VPEs with young people.
athar_applications: Closest available evidence for ATHAR's 13-18 users (in English): younger teens interpret 'likely/almost certain' less consistently, so ATHAR's confidence scale should pair Arabic words with numeric bands and be calibrated separately for 13-15 and 16-18.
limitations: English only; one country; online convenience sample.

title: The interpretation of IPCC probabilistic statements around the world
key_findings: Multinational study (25 samples, 24 countries, 17 languages): laypeople read IPCC verbal terms as closer to 50% than intended.

Adding numerical ranges to the words improved correspondence with intended meanings, differentiated terms better, and made interpretations across languages more similar; patterns were stable across samples and languages.
athar_applications: Strongest cross-linguistic evidence available for G18: whatever Arabic words ATHAR uses for likelihood, display them with numeric ranges ('words + numbers'), which reduces both regression-to-50% and between-language drift.
limitations: Arabic inclusion among the 17 languages not confirmed from the abstract; adults; climate context.

title: Verbal probabilities: Very likely to be somewhat more confusing than numbers
license: CC BY 4.0
key_findings: Online experiment (N = 924) on ICD 203 verbal probability terms: only bracketing the numeric range in the text (e.g., 'very unlikely (05-20%)') substantially improved correspondence (66% vs 32% control); tooltips and linked tables did not.
Also built evidence-based lexicons (membership functions, peak values) of how people map each term to numbers.
athar_applications: UI rule for ATHAR: show the numeric band inline next to the Arabic likelihood word, not in a hover tooltip or help screen.
Method template for ATHAR's own Arabic lexicon study (membership functions per term per age band).
limitations: Adults, English, intelligence-analysis framing.

title: Variability in the interpretation of probability phrases used in Dutch news articles - a risk for miscommunication
publisher: SISSA Medialab (Journal of Science Communication, JCOM)
key_findings: Laypeople and statisticians showed large variability in numeric interpretations of Dutch probability phrases even in neutral context; statisticians did not agree among themselves.
athar_applications: Non-English evidence that the problem is language-general; expertise does not remove it, so ATHAR's authors and reviewers also need the fixed word-to-number table.
limitations: Dutch adults; news phrases.

title: The Interpretation of Verbal Probabilities: A Systematic Literature Review and Meta-Analysis
publisher: IOS Press (German Medical Data Sciences 2022, Studies in Health Technology and Informatics)
key_findings: Meta-analysis of 21 studies (1967-2018; n per study 11-683) covering 35 verbal probability expressions; mean numeric values ranged from about 7% ('impossible') to about 95% ('definite').
Reports broad cross-study consensus following a roughly linear pattern, with high heterogeneity.
athar_applications: Gives anchor values for building an initial Arabic word-to-number scale before ATHAR's own calibration study; heterogeneity means local data are still required.
limitations: Mostly English/German medical contexts; author list partly shown on repository ('and others'); DOI not captured.

title: A Systematic Literature Review of Game-Based Assessment Studies: Trends and Challenges
publisher: IEEE (IEEE Transactions on Learning Technologies, vol. 16, no. 4, pp. 500-515)
key_findings: Reviewed 65 empirical game-based assessment studies (2013-2020): 83% used descriptive statistics, 37% machine learning, and only about 11% knowledge-inference models such as Bayesian networks.
Most frequent limitations: methodology (52%), small samples (46%) and validation issues (37%); only about 14% of tools were publicly available, hampering replication.
athar_applications: The field's evidentiary base is thin; ATHAR's assessment claims should rest on its own validation data (Phase 2-4), and ATHAR can differentiate by publishing its measurement model and reliability results.
limitations: Literature up to 2020; read via arXiv preprint version.

title: Stealth Assessment: A Systematic Review of the Literature
publisher: International Society of the Learning Sciences (Proceedings of ICLS 2023, pp. 1977-1978)
key_findings: 93 stealth-assessment studies identified (grade 3 to adults); of 60 coded, 42 were validation studies, 4 used estimates for adaptivity/feedback, 14 design-only.
Most validation used convergent correlations with external measures (24 of 60); the remaining studies largely did not specify validation.
athar_applications: Using stealth estimates to drive adaptivity (as ATHAR plans) is the least-studied use - ATHAR should validate before letting estimates gate content or reports.
limitations: Two-page in-progress conference summary; author-hosted copy; DOI 10.22318/icls2023.395429 listed on author page but not resolved here.

AUDIT-W2 2026-10-27: DOI 10.22318/icls2023.395429 added: it is listed on the author's official publication page (myweb.fsu.edu/vshute/publications.html) with the same title, authors and pages 1977-1978; doi.org resolves to repository.isls.org/handle/1/10118 (HTTP 403 to automated requests). Counts (93 studies; 60 coded; 42/4/14; 24 convergent) confirmed in the PDF.

title: Getting the First and Second Decimals Right: Psychometrics of Stealth Assessment
publisher: IGI Global (Advances in Educational Technologies and Instructional Design book series)
key_findings: Argues task design sets the 'first decimal' of accuracy and the statistical model only the 'second': with too few tasks, no scoring model yields reliable estimates.

Recommends split-half or cross-validation reliability over game chunks, omega rather than alpha for multi-construct games, and differential task functioning plus observable characteristic plots for fairness; reports convergent correlations around .36-.40 for Physics Playground and .18-.23 for creativity.
athar_applications: Prioritise more and better-targeted observations per skill over model sophistication; ATHAR should choose a simple model (Beta/BKT/IRT) first and invest in task coverage, then use split-half across cases to report reliability.
limitations: Chapter by stealth-assessment developers; examples from one research programme.

title: When is Deep Learning the Best Approach to Knowledge Tracing?
publisher: Journal of Educational Data Mining, vol. 12, no. 3
license: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0
key_findings: Compared learner-performance models on nine real datasets: feature-rich logistic regression led on moderate-size data or many interactions per student; deep knowledge tracing led only on large datasets or where timing mattered.
Markov-process models such as BKT lagged; authors stress model calibration for downstream use.
athar_applications: For ATHAR's early, small-data phase, a logistic/IRT-family model with good features is the defensible default; deep KT only after large datasets; BKT kept for interpretability, not accuracy.
limitations: Tutoring-system data (maths etc.), not narrative games; prediction accuracy is not the same as measurement validity.

title: Measuring the Reliability of Diagnostic Classification Model Examinee Estimates
key_findings: Defines a reliability index for categorical latent variables in diagnostic classification models (DCMs).
Theory and simulation show DCMs give higher examinee-estimate reliability than IRT for tests of the same length, because they estimate fewer latent categories (e.g., master/non-master).
athar_applications: If ATHAR reports coarse mastery states (e.g., not yet / developing / secure) rather than fine scores, it can reach usable reliability with fewer cases - a direct answer to 'reliability with few tasks'.
limitations: Older than the 2018-2026 window but foundational; gains depend on correct attribute specification (Q-matrix); not game data.

title: Knowledge Tracing: A Review of Available Technologies
publisher: University of Southern Mississippi (Journal of Educational Technology Development and Exchange, 14(2))
key_findings: Systematic review of knowledge-tracing models by assumptions, data and algorithms: dynamic Bayesian networks, logistic regression and deep learning dominate.
Most models capture only part of the assumptions about knowledge components and cognition, and nearly all use quiz-style response data.
athar_applications: Game process data (choices, sequences, time) fit poorly into standard KT inputs; ATHAR must define observables carefully (ECD evidence model) before any KT model.
limitations: Descriptive review; small journal.

title: Bayesian Networks in Educational Assessment
publisher: Springer New York (Statistics for Social and Behavioral Sciences)
key_findings: Reference text on building, calibrating and evaluating Bayesian-network evidence models for ECD-based assessments, including model fit and fairness tools used in later stealth-assessment work.
athar_applications: Canonical reference for the Bayes-net option in LEARNER_MASTERY_MODEL; ATHAR's measurement expert should use it to decide whether BN complexity is justified versus simpler IRT/DCM.
limitations: Book read via catalogue metadata only (contents summarised from secondary use in ATH-SRC-1653).

title: Memory-Driven Role-Playing: Evaluation and Enhancement of Persona Knowledge Utilization in LLMs
publisher: Association for Computational Linguistics (Findings of ACL 2026)
license: CC BY 4.0 (paper text, ACL Anthology)
key_findings: Frames persona knowledge as memory the model must retrieve from dialogue context; evaluates four abilities - Anchoring, Selecting, Bounding (staying within the persona's knowledge) and Enacting - across 12 LLMs on a Chinese/English benchmark.
A structured retrieval prompt let small models (e.g., Qwen3-8B) match much larger closed models.
athar_applications: 'Bounding' is exactly ATHAR's knowledge-gate requirement; the four-ability rubric can structure ATHAR's Arabic character test oracles. No Arabic role-play/persona benchmark was found in this search (Chinese/English only, as here).
limitations: Chinese and English only; benchmark not about minors or safety.

title: Meta-analysis indicators of some scientific production in the field of blended learning in the Arab World in the period from 2008 until 2021: analytical-bibliometric study
title_ar: مؤشرات التحليل البعدي لنتائج بعض الإنتاج العلمي في مجال التعلم المدمج في الوطن العربي في الفترة 2008-2021: دراسة تحليلية بيبليومترية
publisher: University of Jordan (Dirasat: Educational Sciences, vol. 50, no. 2, pp. 527-547)
key_findings: Meta-analysis of 55 studies from Arab periodicals (2008-2021) comparing blended with traditional teaching: random-effects mean effect size 1.72, reported as very large, across achievement, motivation, attitude and critical thinking.
athar_applications: Signal of effect-size inflation in Arab-periodical intervention studies (an average near 1.7 is several times international meta-analytic norms of about 0.3-0.4); ATHAR must not cite such pooled values as expected impact and should power studies for 0.2-0.3 [ATH-SRC-0574].
limitations: Author interprets the large effect at face value; study quality, publication bias and design (mostly small quasi-experiments) not verified here.

title: The effect of teaching biology using enquiry strategy on developing of critical thinking and motivation towards learning amongst ninth grade students in Amman
title_ar: أثر تدريس الأحياء باستخدام استراتيجية الاستقصاء في تنمية التفكير الناقد والدافعية نحو التعلم لدى طلاب التاسع الأساسي في عمان
publisher: Journal of Educational Sciences (Cairo University), vol. 27, no. 2, pt. 3, pp. 519-541
key_findings: Quasi-experiment with 50 ninth-grade students in Amman (25 experimental, 25 control, purposive sample): enquiry-based biology teaching group scored higher on a researcher-made critical-thinking test and a motivation measure.
athar_applications: Typical of the available Arab adolescent evidence for G07: very small, non-random, single-site studies with researcher-made instruments and no delayed or transfer measures - insufficient for ATHAR's claims, useful only as a design contrast for ATHAR's own trial.
limitations: n = 50, purposive allocation, no transfer test, instrument validity unclear; journal details from catalogue.

title: Child Protection Centre & Child Helpline 998 - Bahrain National Portal service directory
authors: Kingdom of Bahrain - Information & eGovernment Authority
key_findings: Child Protection Centre (Ministry of Social Development) protects children up to 18 from abuse and neglect; a free child support helpline 998 receives calls from children or others; email and landline contacts listed.
athar_applications: Official Bahrain entry for ATHAR's crisis-exit resource list (register row HL-15).
limitations: Opening hours not stated on the page.

title: Yusr platform - Emergencies and hotlines directory (Qatar Ministry of Social Development and Family)
authors: Ministry of Social Development and Family, Qatar
key_findings: Lists Aman Centre hotline 919 for child and women protection, answering around the clock in several languages with social, psychological and legal counselling; Sidra Medicine child-protection line 40004003 during working hours; unified emergency number 999.
athar_applications: Official Qatar entries for ATHAR's crisis-exit list (register rows HL-13, HL-14).
limitations: Directory page; no mental-health-specific youth line listed on the page read.

title: Protection of Children from Violence - UNICEF Oman
key_findings: States that Oman's child protection hotline (1100) received 784 calls in the first nine months of 2023, mostly about neglect, followed by physical, sexual and psychological abuse; child protection committees handled 1,634 cases.
athar_applications: Confirms Oman's 1100 line for the register (HL-16) and indicates call volumes for a helpline that ATHAR would refer teens to.
limitations: Operator hours taken from a 2020 ministry statement reported by press, not from this page.

title: Embrace - The National Lifeline 1564 (National Emotional Support and Suicide Prevention Hotline)
key_findings: Describes 1564 as Lebanon's national emotional support and suicide prevention hotline, free, confidential and available 24/7, run in collaboration between Embrace and the National Mental Health Programme.
athar_applications: Primary mental-health crisis resource for Lebanon in ATHAR's safety exit (register HL-10).
limitations: Languages and caller age range not stated on page read.

title: Psychiatry / mental health services page - Saudi Ministry of Health (psychological consultation call centre 920033360)
key_findings: The psychological consultation centre of the National Committee/Center for Mental Health Promotion (launched 2013) answers psychological consultations for all groups via 920033360, 08:00-20:00 and Saturday 13:00-20:00, staffed by trained specialists.
athar_applications: Saudi mental-health resource for ATHAR's crisis exit (register HL-02); note it is not 24/7, so the exit text must also give the emergency route.
limitations: Page does not list a youth-specific line; emergency numbers not verified here.

title: The Hotline: a Safety Net to Protect Children (Ministry of Interior 116111 and 'Hemayati' app)
authors: Abu Dhabi Police / UAE Ministry of Interior
key_findings: Official 2016 news item: the UAE Ministry of Interior launched toll-free 116111 for reporting child abuse, alongside the 'Hemayati' app and the MoI Child Protection Centre website.
athar_applications: UAE federal child-abuse reporting route for ATHAR's crisis exit (register HL-03), pending confirmation that the line is still active.
limitations: Dated 2016; current status not re-confirmed (u.ae page returned 404).

title: himaya - Who we are (hotline 03 414 964 and e-helpline)
key_findings: Lists a child-abuse hotline (03 414 964) and an online e-helpline form; states that himaya is mandated by the Ministry of Justice to handle legal protection cases in the North Governorate.
athar_applications: Lebanon child-protection reporting route for ATHAR (register HL-11), complementing the 1564 mental-health line.
limitations: Hours not stated; NGO rather than state service.

title: Child protection hotline 'suspended' (Kuwait 147)
key_findings: Reported (11 Feb 2019) that the 147 child-abuse hotline announced by the Ministry of Health was not in service when called, and that the ministry said the project had been postponed.
athar_applications: Reason the Kuwait row (HL-12) is marked needs_live_test: a later 2024 MOH statement (Al Rai) says a 24/7 line 147 operates, but a listed helpline that does not answer is worse than none in a crisis exit.
limitations: Journalism; superseded at least in part by later ministry statements.
